accepted_established_edges.statement: The Pantheon builders incorporated coarse lightweight volcanic aggregate into the upper dome, laying tuff and scoria in alternating courses.
accepted_established_edges.scope: Use of Rome’s lightweight coarse-aggregate construction process in the upper dome of the Pantheon.
accepted_established_edges.caveats: The route by which the builders acquired the technique remains unknown. A modern finite-element model predicted lower peak hoop tension with graded densities across the whole structure. The effect of the crown scoria alone remains unquantified by that comparison.

evidence.locator: p. 213, paragraph beginning “La cupola, impostata sull’ultimo cornicione interno”
evidence.supports: From the 1929–1934 restoration, Terenzio directly describes the horizontal courses of the Pantheon vault and their composition, including alternating tuff and lightweight volcanic scoria in its upper zone.

evidence.locator: pp. 707–709 and 711–713, figs. 2 and 3b
evidence.supports: Rome’s practice of using lightweight caementa is documented in sampled vaults. The authors identify yellow tuff and scoria in the Basilica Ulpia fragment and compare them with the same materials in the Pantheon crown.

evidence.locator: pp. 79–82, §§3–4, figs. 1, 3 and 5, fragment No. 10
evidence.supports: The field study details the alternating coarse aggregate courses in the Basilica Ulpia fragment.

evidence.locator: pp. 26–29, models 5 and 6 and maximum-tension table
evidence.supports: The graded-density version produced lower peak hoop tension in the authors’ uncracked finite-element comparison. Their input on material grading came from De Fine Licht’s survey.

accepted_established_edges.statement: Babbage adapted the Jacquard loom’s method of using successive perforated cards to select mechanical actions. In his Analytical Engine design, separate card strings specified the arithmetic operations and which columns would supply or receive numbers.
accepted_established_edges.scope: Transfer of a control method from working looms into an engineering design for calculation.

evidence.locator: Footnote 3, December 1839 letter to Arago
evidence.supports: In the committee’s published excerpt, Babbage credits the Jacquard system he used as the basis for communicating calculation instructions to his engine.

evidence.locator: Menabrea, pp. 677–678, and Lovelace, Note E, p. 720
evidence.supports: Menabrea credits Jacquard’s apparatus and explains the two card functions. Lovelace describes the Engine’s prism presenting cards to lever bundles and turning backward to reuse a sequence.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3, chapter PDF pp. 5 and 18 (whole PDF pp. 27 and 40), especially nn. 31, 41–42
evidence.supports: Collier’s examination of Babbage’s working notebooks and drawings traces the shift from studded drum control to the Jacquard card method, citing the earlier 1836 notes.

evidence.locator: pp. 197 and 214 (§12); p. 217 (§14 and acknowledgments)
evidence.supports: Bromley identifies borrowing from the Jacquard loom and reconstructs the use of ribbon-linked card strings and the Engine’s distinct operation and variable card functions from the surviving designs.

unresolved_edges.statement: Did hominins use the recurring fires identified in Area B to cook fish?
unresolved_edges.scope: Gesher Benot Ya‘aqov, Area B Layer II-6 levels 1–7, including 4b.
unresolved_edges.finding: The studies examine the same eight horizons and share the burnt-flint evidence. Some tested teeth show changes consistent with moderate heating, and the published density maps place fish remains near likely hearths.
unresolved_edges.alternatives: Later heating of fish refuse near a fire could produce a spatial association. The fish study argues against direct disposal into a hot fire on the basis of the tooth measurements and scarcity of charred bone.
unresolved_edges.caveats: The hotspot tests measure clustering within the fish assemblage. Spatial overlap with burnt flint is shown in density maps, often using finds recorded by excavation unit. A separate assessment of the thermal and spatial evidence for cooking is still needed.

evidence.locator: Table 1, section 3 and Fig. 2
evidence.supports: The eight horizons with burnt-flint clusters match the stratigraphic scope of the fish study.

evidence.locator: Figs. 4–5, Discussion and Supplementary Text E
evidence.supports: The authors infer cooking from the heating comparison and spatial overlap. They consider the alternative of consumption of raw or dried fish followed by disposal into a fire.

unresolved_edges.statement: Did Canal 3 supply water to fields on the lower bench during Tierra Blanca cultivation?
unresolved_edges.scope: Canal 3 and the buried lower-bench field at Quebrada sin Nombre-1.
unresolved_edges.timing: The Canal 3 fill age falls within the 2011 Tierra Blanca phase interval. The lower-bench field's age remains open.
unresolved_edges.finding: The excavators inferred that the canals watered the bench from local topography and sediment. Independent evidence for the field's connection to Canal 3 remains unavailable.

evidence.locator: pp. 17242–17244, Figs. 1–3 and discussion of the lower bench
evidence.supports: The canals lie above a lower bench identified as a probable field location. The report gives a fill age for Canal 3 and describes the buried field as undated.

unresolved_edges.statement: Can a documented crop lineage or route link the early Xihuatoxtla maize use to the maize processed by the Nahua?
unresolved_edges.scope: Cultivated maize is the material required by the recorded Nahua practice. This candidate asks whether the earlier Xihuatoxtla witness can be connected to that particular material history.
unresolved_edges.caveats: Modern genetic comparisons are regional in scope. The local grain lineage, supply route and transmission of the cooking practice remain unresolved.
unresolved_edges.timing: Use of the crop is archaeologically attested in the Early Holocene. The cooking practice is attested for the Nahua by the completion of the manuscript in 1577.
unresolved_edges.finding: The Florentine Codex identifies the input as maize, and genetic and archaeological evidence support a regional history of domestication. Neither identifies the particular variety or its route from an Early Holocene population to the Nahua cooks.

evidence.locator: Abstract, Xihuatoxtla maize by 8,700 cal BP
evidence.supports: The Central Balsas site documents early use of the domesticated crop.

evidence.locator: Figs. 1–2 and Cradle of Maize Domestication, pp. 6081–6083
evidence.supports: Independent genetic analysis of modern samples supports a shared crop ancestry within Balsas teosinte for sampled maize landraces, including samples from central Mexico.

evidence.locator: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 4 folio 69r, Nahuatl transcription and Anderson–Dibble English translation
evidence.supports: The folio describes maize previously cooked with lime being washed as part of food preparation; the manuscript is dated 1577.

evidence.locator: §3 and §§7–8, including control trials
evidence.supports: Experiments treat whole maize kernels as the raw material and compare lime-treated maize with non-alkaline cooking controls.

unresolved_edges.statement: Did Tang flying-money certificates contribute to the emergence of Sichuan jiaozi?
unresolved_edges.scope: Possible institutional influence on Sichuan jiaozi specifically.
unresolved_edges.finding: The Yuan-era Song shi tentatively traces both huizi and jiaozi to Tang flying cash. Its account names no intermediary or transmission route for the Sichuan bills. Li Dao documents the local shift from private issue to a public office, but that explains a later change within Sichuan.

evidence.locator: Juan 181, Food and Finance III, opening of Huizi (會子)
evidence.supports: The opening sentence proposes an antecedent shared by huizi and jiaozi, without recording how it reached Sichuan issuers.

evidence.locator: Juan 54, Food and Finance IV, paragraph beginning 時商賈至京師
evidence.supports: Describes a long-distance mechanism for redeeming deposited funds with matching tallies.

evidence.locator: Juan 101, Tiansheng 1, eleventh month, wuwu (戊午)
evidence.supports: Documents a local trade medium and the takeover of its administration.

evidence.locator: Chronology, approximately 810 CE
evidence.supports: Suggests flying money as a possible precursor of banknotes in general.

unresolved_edges.statement: Did the wave models taught by Isao Eknilang and Thomas Bokin contribute to Joel's navigation on the return from Ujae to Kwajalein?
unresolved_edges.scope: Recalled teaching on the 2006 return leg
unresolved_edges.finding: Genz's firsthand account attributes Joel's selective reading of sea conditions to both models. WAM's account also draws on Genz's testimony. Seek a separate account from Joel or Alson Kelen about how Joel used the models on the return leg.

evidence.locator: pp. 13, 29–30, Introduction and The Stern Test of Landfall
evidence.supports: Documents instruction from Eknilang before the voyage and Bokin's explanation by weaving a meto into his sitting mat at Ujae, before the return leg.

evidence.locator: pp. 13, 29–32, The Stern Test of Landfall and fig. 7
evidence.supports: Dates the voyage to 2006 and distinguishes limited wavefinding outbound from wave piloting on the return leg, when Joel had both models in mind.

evidence.locator: Participant account beginning “On that first voyage in 2006”
evidence.supports: Genz names the itinerary, year and purpose of the trial, and reports discussion with Thomas Bokin on Ujae.

unresolved_edges.statement: Did Good’s interaction and Fourier methods inform Tukey’s early factorisation or the derivation Cooley and Tukey published in 1965?
unresolved_edges.caveats: The 1958 paper’s one-dimensional reduction uses coprime factors. The 1965 algorithm handles repeated factors and cites Good’s more general idea of using sparse matrix factors. The authors’ 1993 sequence places Cooley’s inquiry about Good after his radix-2 implementation. Good separately recalled a brief 1956 conversation with Tukey, leaving Tukey’s earlier knowledge possible and the mathematical influence uncertain.

evidence.supports: Good’s prime-factor reduction uses pairwise coprime lengths and permutations grounded in the Chinese remainder theorem.

evidence.locator: pp. 297–298, introduction and equations (3)–(8); p. 301, reference 2
evidence.supports: Credits Good’s methods for sparse matrix factorisation, gives a different derivation for complex Fourier sums, and allows repeated factors.

evidence.locator: pp. 8–9, radix-2 program, patentability inquiry and publication
evidence.supports: The authors recall that Tukey named Good during a prior-art inquiry after Cooley’s radix-2 programming and before preparation of the coauthored draft.

evidence.locator: pp. 15–16, Good’s remarks on the FFT
evidence.supports: Good recalls giving Tukey a brief description during a December 1956 visit and does not specify which mathematical ideas he conveyed.

evidence.locator: p. 265, Introduction
evidence.supports: Distinguishes the two algorithms. Its attribution of influence comes from its reading of the 1965 paper.

supported_circumstances.statement: Ada Lovelace published her English translation of Luigi Federico Menabrea’s description of the Analytical Engine with her own notes. She explained how reversing the card feed would let the design reuse a sequence of cards.

supported_circumstances.record_name: Gesher Benot Ya‘aqov inferred fish cooking
supported_circumstances.statement: In eight Area B occupation horizons in Layer II-6 (levels 1–7, including 4b), fish remains consist predominantly of pharyngeal teeth and overlap spatially with burnt flint concentrations. X-ray diffraction on selected teeth yielded patterns consistent with moderate heating in some specimens. Zohar and colleagues inferred that hominins cooked fish at the lakeside site.
supported_circumstances.qualification: Intentional cooking is inferred from the pattern of remains and experimental comparisons. The measurements cannot identify a cooking apparatus or technique.

evidence.locator: Abstract, Results and Fig. 1
evidence.supports: The eight Area B occupation horizons at the site dated to about 0.78 million years ago preserve abundant fish teeth and few fish bones, unlike the natural-death comparison in Area A.

evidence.locator: Figs. 4–5 and Supplementary Texts D–E
evidence.supports: Tooth mineral comparisons support moderate heating for some sampled teeth. The density maps compare clusters of fish remains and burnt flint in the same occupation horizons.

supported_circumstances.facet: Tierra Blanca phase, c. 7800–5000 cal BP (5850–3050 BCE)
supported_circumstances.statement: Archaeologists interpret the Tierra Blanca evidence in the Ñanchoc Valley as a shift toward more intensive cultivation, with fields worked by multiple households and small-scale irrigation in the valley.
supported_circumstances.qualification: The field below the dated canals remains undated, and the crops grown there are unidentified. Directly dated cotton from CA-09-71 came from a house floor.

evidence.locator: Chapter 9, public summary, final paragraph; same volume, chapter 1, dating convention
evidence.supports: The synthesis dates Tierra Blanca to 7800–5000 calibrated BP and describes the shift from single-family gardens to multifamily fields and canal systems in the upper valley.

evidence.locator: pp. 19622–19623, site context preceding Fig. 1
evidence.supports: The study reports plant remains, planting plots, stone hoes and small irrigation canals across Tierra Blanca contexts. The analyzed teeth come from earlier Las Pircas occupations.

evidence.locator: pp. 1890–1891, crop descriptions and Fig. 5; p. 1892, Table 1, CA-09-71
evidence.supports: The paper reports peanut remains and quinoa-like chenopods at Tierra Blanca sites. Cotton recovered from a house floor at CA-09-71 dates to 6278–5948 cal BP.

evidence.locator: pp. 17243–17244, Fig. 3 and discussion of the lower bench and garden sites
evidence.supports: The lower-bench agricultural field contained hoe-like implements and is undated. The probable earlier garden furrows at CA-09-27 and CA-09-52 are on a separate fan.

supported_circumstances.record_name: Alkaline cooking of maize at San Bartolo
supported_circumstances.statement: Starch spherulites in sealed refuse deposits associated with Structures 192 and 195 B/C match residues produced by experimental lime treatment of maize. The excavators interpret the residues as likely discarded cooking liquid.
supported_circumstances.qualification: The dating is contextual and the charcoal ranges include intervals outside the authors’ preferred estimate. The deposits establish where the residues ended up. The precise cooking location, recipe and date of invention remain unresolved.

evidence.locator: §3, Table 1 and Figs. 3–6
evidence.supports: The sealed household refuse contexts and the authors’ most likely interval of pit use, c. 770–895 cal CE.
Microscopic structure and a calcium-rich elemental signature support the identification. The authors infer that alkaline cooking liquid may have been discarded into the pits.

evidence.locator: §3 and §§7–8, including control trials
evidence.supports: Lime-treated maize yielded distinctive spherulites under these experimental conditions. Non-alkaline controls did not. The archaeological study shares an author with the experiment.

supported_circumstances.record_name: Toothed gearing in the Hellenistic Greek world
supported_circumstances.facet: c. 225 BCE to before the wreck (probably 60 ± 10 BCE)
supported_circumstances.statement: Freeth and colleagues estimate that the Greek geared device was made around the end of the second century BC. The date of construction remains uncertain. Its eclipse dial represented a 223-lunar-month cycle and marked possible solar or lunar eclipses. About one third of that scale survives. The upper back dial displayed a 19-year calendar of 235 lunar months in a five-turn spiral, consistent with the count in the back-cover inscription. Fragment B preserves part of the scale and part of the pointer, including the guiding pin that followed the gap between turns. Anastasiou and colleagues reconstruct the damaged mounting as a pointer that slid through its hub as the shaft turned. The final gear that drove the pointer is missing.
supported_circumstances.qualification: Jones finds the letter forms compatible with manufacture from about 225 BCE up to the shipwreck. The latest year represents the later end of his probable wreck date, based on ceramics and coins. Both endpoints are approximate.

evidence.supports: constructed around the end of the second century bc
evidence.locator: Abstract

evidence.supports: The spiral scale represents 223 lunar months, includes eclipse-possibility glyphs, and is about one third extant.
evidence.locator: Section 1, The Mechanism’s eclipse function
§1, pp. 1–2, construction chronology; §2, pp. 3–4, Fig. 1 and Back Cover Inscription II.3
evidence.supports: The back-cover inscription gives 235 divisions. The surviving divisions accord with a five-turn spiral for the lunar months of the 19-year calendar. Jones finds the letter forms compatible with manufacture from about 225 BCE to before the shipwreck, which he estimates at 60 ± 10 BCE.

evidence.locator: §1, PDF p. 1 and Fig. 1; §2.1, PDF pp. 3–5 and Figs. 3–5; §2.2, PDF pp. 5–7 and Fig. 6
evidence.supports: CT images show part of the Metonic spiral, pointer and damaged shaft mounting in Fragment B. The authors reconstruct a pin guided by the spiral slot and a pointer sliding through its rotating hub, using the inscription as a check. The last drive gear is missing.
